10550: Meringue is a light, sweet, white, foamy mixture made by beating egg whites with sugar until the mixture becomes thick, glossy, and holds its shape. It is used widely in baking and dessert-making.

To understand meringue, picture what happens when you whip egg whites vigorously. The liquid egg whites trap millions of tiny air bubbles and transform into a stiff, white foam — almost like shaving cream, but made of eggs. When you add sugar to this and keep beating, the sugar stabilizes that foam, making it smooth, glossy, and strong enough to hold a shape. That final mixture — airy, white, and sweet — is meringue.

So meringue is a stable foam of air trapped in egg whites and held together by sugar. It is almost weightless, because most of its volume is just air.
What it looks, feels, and tastes like

• Before baking: Thick, glossy, brilliant white, and soft — almost like very stiff whipped cream.
  • After baking: The outside becomes crisp and dry, like a light shell, while the inside can remain slightly soft and chewy, similar to a marshmallow. The colour turns from pure white to a pale ivory or light golden-brown.
  • Taste: Very sweet, clean, and delicate. It melts gently on the tongue. It has almost no flavour beyond sweetness and a faint egginess.
  • Texture in the mouth: Baked meringue tends to be airy and crisp, crumbling or dissolving easily as you eat it.

Meringue isn't just one fixed thing — chefs make it in three different ways, and each produces a slightly different result. You'll encounter these terms if you read baking recipes or food writing:

1. French meringue (the basic, everyday kind)
Raw egg whites are beaten with fine sugar until stiff and glossy. This is the simplest version to make, but it is also the most fragile — it must be baked soon after making. This is what most people at home make.

2. Swiss meringue (the smooth, silky kind)
The egg whites and sugar are gently warmed together in a bowl placed over simmering water, whisked the entire time, and then beaten into a thick, glossy foam. The gentle heat makes it more stable and gives it a smoother, denser texture than French meringue.

3. Italian meringue (the cooked, very stable kind)
Very hot sugar syrup — cooked to a precise temperature — is poured in a thin stream into egg whites that are already being beaten. The heat from the syrup partially cooks the egg whites, making this the most stable and safest type (since it's already been heated). Professional bakers and pastry chefs favour it for toppings and fillings because it holds its shape beautifully and won't deflate easily.
How meringue is used in cooking and baking

Meringue plays several distinct roles in the kitchen:

As a topping: Perhaps the most iconic use is on top of lemon meringue pie, where soft peaks of meringue are spread over a lemon custard filling, then briefly baked or torched until the surface turns golden-brown with slightly charred tips. The contrast between the tangy filling and the sweet, soft meringue is the point of the dish.

As baked cookies or shells: Meringue can be piped or spooned into small mounds on a baking tray and baked very slowly at a low temperature until completely dry and crisp all the way through. These are called meringues (the small baked pieces) or meringue cookies. They are very light, crisp, and sweet.

As the base of Pavlova: Pavlova is a famous dessert made from a large round of meringue baked so that the outside is crisp but the inside stays soft and marshmallow-like. It is then topped with whipped cream and fresh fruit. Pavlova is named after the Russian ballerina Anna Pavlova and is especially popular in Australia and New Zealand.

As a component in other desserts: Meringue is also an ingredient inside many other preparations — folded into mousses to make them light and airy, used as the filling in macarons (the delicate French sandwich cookies), spread over ice cream in Baked Alaska (a spectacular dessert where ice cream is covered in meringue and then briefly baked or torched so the outside browns while the ice cream stays frozen inside), and mixed into various buttercreams to create a light, silky cake frosting.
A critical property: meringue and moisture

One essential thing to know about meringue is that it is extremely sensitive to humidity and moisture. Sugar naturally attracts water from the surrounding air. Because meringue contains so much sugar, it readily absorbs moisture — and when it does, it softens, becomes sticky, or starts to "weep" (tiny drops of liquid form on its surface). This is why:

  • Meringue is best made on a dry day, not a humid one.
  • Baked meringues go soft if stored improperly or left out in a humid environment.
  • Lemon meringue pie often needs to be eaten the same day, because the moisture from the filling and the air gradually makes the meringue layer weep and soften.
How the word is used in sentences

The noun "meringue" works in two slightly different ways:

  • As an uncountable noun (referring to the substance or mixture itself): "She spread a thick layer of meringue over the pie." / "The recipe calls for meringue made with three egg whites."
  • As a countable noun (referring to an individual baked meringue piece): "He ate two meringues from the bakery." / "She decorated the cake with small meringues."

When you see "a meringue" or "meringues" (plural), it almost always refers to the individual baked pieces — the cookies or shells. When you see "meringue" without an article, it usually refers to the mixture or the concept.

Meringue is a delicate, airy, sweet preparation made from beaten egg whites and sugar. It can be soft and cloud-like, used as a topping; crisp and dry, eaten as a cookie; or marshmallow-soft inside a baked shell. It appears in a remarkable range of desserts — from pies to cakes to standalone sweets — and is one of the fundamental building blocks of Western baking and pastry-making. Its defining qualities are its lightness (because it is mostly air), its whiteness, its sweetness, and its fragility in the face of moisture.
10551:
Merit means genuine worth — the quality of something (or someone) that makes it truly good, valuable, or deserving of recognition, reward, or approval.

The key word here is genuine. Merit is not about luck, charm, connections, or appearances. It is about actual, real, earned quality. When something has merit, it has earned its value honestly, through what it actually is or what someone actually did.

Think of it this way: if a student gets an A because they studied hard, understood the material, and wrote an excellent paper — that grade is based on merit. But if they got an A because the teacher is their relative — that has nothing to do with merit.

1. Merit as a general quality (uncountable)

This is when "merit" is used without a number — you can't say "one merit, two merits" in this sense. It refers to the overall worthiness or goodness of something.

  • "Her proposal has merit." → Her proposal is genuinely good; it deserves to be taken seriously.
  • "The idea lacks merit." → The idea isn't actually good; it doesn't deserve approval.
  • "There is merit in what you're saying." → What you're saying has some real truth or value to it.

In this sense, merit is almost like a stamp of genuine quality. Saying something "has merit" is a measured, thoughtful compliment — it means this deserves serious attention because it's actually good.

2. Merits as specific good qualities (countable, plural)

Here, "merits" refers to the individual good points or advantages of something — the specific reasons why something is worth supporting or choosing.

  • "We discussed the merits of each plan." → We talked about the good points that each plan has.
  • "Every idea should be judged on its own merits." → Every idea should be evaluated based on its own specific good qualities.

In this plural sense, "merits" is often paired with "drawbacks" or "flaws" — because when you're making a fair judgment, you weigh the good (merits) against the bad (flaws).
The Most Important Phrase: "On its merits"

One of the most common and important ways "merit" is used is in the phrase "judge something on its merits" (or "on its own merits"). This means: evaluate something purely based on what it actually is — its real qualities, facts, and substance — without letting bias, emotion, personal relationships, or outside factors influence your judgment.

  • "The application should be reviewed on its merits, not on who submitted it."
  • "Let's evaluate each candidate on their own merits."

This phrase carries a strong sense of fairness and objectivity. When someone says "judge it on its merits," they are asking for a clean, honest evaluation.
The Deeper Idea Behind Merit: Deserving

The concept at the foundation of "merit" is deserving. Something that has merit deserves the good thing it receives. This makes merit different from words like "quality" or "value" in a subtle but important way.

  • A painting might have value simply because it's old or rare — even if it isn't particularly good.
  • But a painting has merit because it is genuinely skillful, moving, or beautiful — because it has earned admiration through what it actually is.

Merit implies a kind of justice or fairness — the idea that good things should go to what truly earns them.

Understanding what a word doesn't mean is just as important as understanding what it does. Merit is not:

  • Luck — Something doesn't have merit just because it succeeded by chance.
  • Popularity — Something isn't meritorious just because many people like it.
  • Privilege or connections — A person doesn't have merit in a role just because of who they know or who their family is.
  • Surface appeal — Something that looks impressive but is hollow underneath does not have merit.

Merit is always about substance over surface.
Common Collocations (Words You'll Often See with "Merit")

These are words and phrases that naturally appear alongside "merit":

  • Has merit / lacks merit — the most basic uses
  • On its merits / on their merits — judging fairly and objectively
  • Of merit — worthy, significant ("a work of merit," "an artist of merit")
  • Merit-based — decided according to actual quality or ability ("a merit-based promotion")
  • On the merits — especially in legal or formal discussions, meaning based on the actual substance of a case or argument, not on technicalities
  • Merits and drawbacks / merits and demerits — the good points and the bad points weighed together

In everyday conversation:

  • "Your complaint has merit — the service was genuinely poor."
  • "I see the merit in your suggestion, but I think we should also consider the risks."

In academic or professional writing:

  • "The argument, while interesting, lacks sufficient merit to overturn the existing evidence."
  • "Candidates will be selected strictly on merit."

In legal or formal contexts:

  • "The judge dismissed the case on the merits." (The case was decided based on its actual substance and facts.)
  • "The committee will assess each application on its own merits."

In everyday evaluation:

  • "Both approaches have their merits — the first is faster, and the second is more thorough."
  • "We spent the meeting debating the merits of switching to a new system."
A Simple Way to Remember It

Whenever you see or hear the word "merit," ask yourself: Is this thing genuinely good? Does it deserve what it's getting?

If yes — it has merit.
If it only seems good, or got something for the wrong reasons — merit doesn't apply.

Merit is the honest answer to the question: "Does this actually deserve it?"
10552:
To merit something means to deserve it — because the thing, person, situation, or action is good enough, serious enough, or important enough to justify that response.

Think of it this way: when something merits a reaction, it means that reaction is not random or excessive — it is earned by the nature of the thing itself. The thing pulls the response toward it, the way a truly great performance pulls applause toward it, or the way a serious problem pulls urgent attention toward it.
A Simple Way to Feel It

Imagine you are a judge deciding whether something should receive a certain treatment. If you conclude "yes, this thing is significant/good/serious enough to deserve this," you are thinking in the language of merit.

"This issue merits our attention" means: this issue is serious or important enough that giving it our attention is the right, justified thing to do.

This is important: merit is not only used for good things. It works in both directions.

Positive: "Her years of hard work merit recognition." (Her work is good enough to deserve recognition.)

Negative: "His dishonest conduct merits a formal investigation." (His behavior is serious enough to deserve being investigated.)

The word itself doesn't judge whether the outcome is a reward or a consequence — it simply says the outcome is justified by the quality or nature of the thing.
Grammar: How to Use It in a Sentence

The structure is clean and consistent:

Something + merits + (noun or -ing verb)

The subject is the thing being judged. What follows is what it deserves.

With a noun: "This plan merits serious consideration." / "The discovery merits praise."

With an -ing verb: "The situation merits examining closely." / "The complaint merits looking into."

You will almost never say "I merit" or "you merit" in everyday use. The subject is typically a thing, a situation, an action, or an idea — not a person directly. You'd say "her courage merits admiration," not "she merits admiration" (though the second is technically possible and sometimes used).
Register: Where and When This Word Is Used

Merit as a verb is formal or semi-formal. You will see it in professional writing, academic papers, journalism, reports, and careful speech. It would sound odd in casual conversation.

Casual: "That deserves a second look."
Formal: "That merits a second look."

Both mean the same thing, but merit carries more weight and precision. If you see it in an article or a report, it signals that the writer is being deliberate and analytical.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Deserve is the closest synonym. The difference is one of register, not meaning. "Deserve" is universal — you can use it anywhere, formal or informal, with people or things. "Merit" is more formal and is more commonly used with things, situations, and abstract subjects rather than people.

Warrant is also very close. The subtle difference is that warrant leans slightly more toward logical justification — it suggests that something calls for or requires a response. Merit leans slightly more toward the idea of inherent worth or quality that earns a response. In practice, the two overlap heavily and are often interchangeable: "This merits further discussion" and "This warrants further discussion" mean almost exactly the same thing.

Earn implies active effort — someone worked for something and got it as a result. Merit does not require effort; even a passive situation can merit a response simply because of what it is.

Certain things are very commonly "merited" in formal English. Knowing these will help you recognize and use the word naturally:

merit attention — this topic merits attention.
merit consideration — the proposal merits serious consideration.
merit discussion — the findings merit further discussion.
merit investigation — the allegations merit a thorough investigation.
merit recognition / praise — the achievement merits recognition.
merit concern — the trend merits concern.
merit a closer look — the data merits a closer look.
merit special mention — one point merits special mention.
A Final Clarifying Note on Tense

You can use merit in past or present tense, and both work naturally:

Present: "The question merits careful thought." (Right now, it is serious enough to deserve thought.)
Past: "The performance merited a standing ovation." (It was good enough to deserve one, and perhaps received one.)

One subtle thing: when used in the present tense ("merits"), it often implies the deserved thing hasn't happened yet — you are making a case that it should. When used in the past tense ("merited"), it more often reflects on something that was deserved, whether or not it was received.

If you want one sentence to carry the whole meaning with you: to merit something is to be worthy of it by virtue of what you are or what you've done, in a way that makes the response justified, not arbitrary. It is a word for situations where there is a real, earned connection between the thing and the response it draws — where you can look at both and say: yes, that fits. That is deserved.
10553:
A meritocracy is a system — a society, an organization, a government, or a workplace — where people succeed, earn rewards, and gain power or positions based purely on their merit. Merit means a combination of your abilities, your talent, your effort, and your results.

In a meritocracy, the question asked is simple: What can you do, and how well can you do it? If your answer is impressive, you rise. If it isn't, you don't. Your family name, your wealth, your social connections, your gender, your race — none of that is supposed to matter.
What the Opposite Looks Like (So the Definition Clicks Better)

To truly understand meritocracy, it helps to see what it stands against.

Imagine a kingdom where the king's son automatically becomes the next king, regardless of whether he is wise, capable, or fit to rule. That is an aristocracy — power by birth. Now imagine a company where a manager hires his nephew for a role, even though another candidate was far more skilled. That is nepotism — advancement through personal connections. Or picture a country where whoever has the most money gets to make the rules. That is a plutocracy — power through wealth.

A meritocracy says: none of that is fair. The job should go to the best candidate. The leadership role should go to the most capable person. The prize should go to whoever earned it most. The starting point of your life — your family, your luck of birth — should not determine where you end up.

Think of a few simple, concrete situations:

A university that admits students purely based on their academic performance and demonstrated ability — not on whether their parents donated money or went to that school — is operating as a meritocracy.

A company that promotes employees based on their performance reviews, the quality of their work, and the results they deliver — rather than on how friendly they are with the boss — is trying to be a meritocracy.

A sports team that selects players entirely based on their athletic skill and on-field performance, with no favoritism, is meritocratic.

The common thread: the best person for the role gets the role, because they are the best.
Meritocracy as an Ideal vs. Meritocracy in Reality

Here is where things get genuinely interesting — and important.

Meritocracy is, first and foremost, an ideal. It describes how a system should work. Most modern democratic societies and corporations claim to be meritocratic. But whether they actually are is a completely different question, and a deeply debated one.

The central problem is this: merit does not develop in a vacuum. A child born into a wealthy family gets access to better schools, private tutors, a stable home, a strong network of influential people, and more time to develop skills without worrying about survival. A child born into poverty may have just as much raw potential, but far fewer resources to develop it. So when both children compete as adults, the wealthy one has a massive head start — and winning a race you started ahead in does not necessarily mean you are the most talented or hardworking. It may just mean you had better conditions.

This is why critics argue that calling a society "meritocratic" can actually be misleading or even harmful — because it implies the playing field is level when it often is not. It can cause people to conclude that those at the bottom of society deserve to be there because they simply lacked enough merit, which ignores the role of structural disadvantages, luck, and inherited privilege. This can make a society less sympathetic to inequality rather than more motivated to fix it.

There is another layer of difficulty: what exactly counts as merit?

Is it intelligence? Hard work? Creativity? Emotional wisdom? The ability to score well on standardized tests? Different societies, industries, and cultures answer this question differently. A system that rewards one type of intelligence may completely overlook another. Someone brilliant at building things with their hands may be undervalued in a system that prizes academic credentials. Someone with extraordinary social and leadership skills may be passed over in a system that only measures technical output.

So even if a meritocracy is working as intended, it is still making a judgment call about which qualities it values — and that choice is not neutral.

You will encounter "meritocracy" in discussions about politics, education, business, and social equality. Here is how it typically appears in context:

"Silicon Valley often prides itself on being a meritocracy, where any talented engineer can rise to the top regardless of background."

"Critics argue that true meritocracy is impossible without first addressing unequal access to education."

"The scholarship program was designed to make the university's admissions process more of a genuine meritocracy."

A meritocracy is a system where advancement, reward, and power are determined by a person's own abilities and efforts — not by inherited privilege, wealth, social class, or personal connections. It is widely considered a just and fair ideal. However, its real-world application is complicated by the fact that people do not start life on equal footing, that "merit" itself is not always easy or objective to define, and that believing a system is meritocratic can sometimes mask the unfair advantages that already exist within it.

Understanding meritocracy, then, means holding two things in mind at once: it is a genuinely appealing principle worth striving for, and it is also a concept that deserves honest scrutiny every time someone claims it has been achieved.
10554:
"Meritocratic" describes any system, process, organization, or society that rewards people based on their actual abilities, effort, and achievements — and nothing else.

The word comes from the concept of merit, which means the real value of what you can do and what you accomplish through your skills and hard work. If something is meritocratic, your success in it is determined by how good you are at what you do and the results you produce. Your family background, wealth, social connections, gender, age, race, or who you know — none of that is supposed to matter.
A picture to make it clear

Imagine two schools, both selecting students for a prestigious program.

School A selects students based on which families donated the most money to the school, or based on whether their parents are alumni.

School B selects students purely by holding a rigorous exam — open to every applicant equally — and admitting the top scorers, regardless of who their parents are or how much money their family has.

School B is operating a meritocratic selection process. The deciding factor is demonstrated ability, nothing more.
What meritocratic stands in contrast to

Understanding what meritocratic opposes is one of the clearest ways to grasp its meaning.

In an aristocratic or class-based system, the family you were born into determines your rank in society. A nobleman's son becomes a nobleman regardless of his talents. In a system plagued by nepotism, a boss hires their cousin over a far more qualified stranger. In a system of cronyism, your powerful friends are your ticket to the top. In a purely seniority-based system, the employee who has simply been around the longest gets promoted, even if a newer employee vastly outperforms them.

Every one of these systems rewards something other than merit. Meritocratic is the direct opposite of all of them. It says: the only thing that should open the door for you is what you can genuinely do and what you actually achieve.
How the word is used in sentences

"Meritocratic" is an adjective, so it modifies nouns. Here are common ways it appears:

Before a noun:
"She believes in a meritocratic workplace, where promotions go to whoever performs best." Here, it describes what kind of workplace she values.

"The sports team's selection process is entirely meritocratic — only skill and fitness scores determine who makes the squad." Here, it describes the selection process.

After a linking verb:
"The hiring system at that company is genuinely meritocratic." This tells you what the system is like.

When someone calls something meritocratic, they are usually signaling that it is fair, objective, and based on real performance — as opposed to favoritism or privilege.
The positive side of the word

In most everyday use, "meritocratic" carries a positive, even idealistic tone. A meritocratic society is one most people consider just and fair — one where a child born into poverty can rise to the top through sheer talent and hard work, where no ceiling exists except the limit of your own ability and dedication. It is the idea that the best person gets the job, the most talented student gets the scholarship, and the hardest-working employee gets the promotion.

This is why the word is often used to describe values or goals that people and organizations are proud of. "We run a meritocratic company" is meant to say: we are fair, we don't play favorites, we reward excellence.
The critical side of the word

Here is where the word gets more interesting and nuanced. While meritocracy sounds beautifully fair in theory, a significant debate exists about whether truly meritocratic systems can exist in the real world, and whether calling something meritocratic is always an honest label.

The key challenge is this: people do not start from equal positions. A child born into a wealthy family gets access to better schools, private tutors, a wider network, and more time to develop their skills — advantages that have nothing to do with their own merit. When that child then "wins" in a system that tests their skills, are they winning purely on merit, or partly on the advantages they inherited? Critics argue that calling such a system meritocratic ignores the deeply unequal starting line.

There is also the question of how merit is defined. If a company defines "talent" using criteria that happen to favor one type of person (a particular background, a particular style of communication, a particular way of thinking), that definition quietly advantages some people while appearing neutral and objective. The system looks meritocratic on the surface but may embed hidden bias in what it chooses to reward.

Finally, luck matters in ways that pure merit cannot account for. Being in the right place at the right time, having a chance encounter with the right person, or being born in the right era — these things shape outcomes alongside talent and effort.

This is why you will sometimes hear "meritocratic" used critically or even skeptically. A journalist might write: "The company claims to be meritocratic, but its leadership is overwhelmingly made up of graduates from just two elite universities." The word, in that context, is being questioned rather than celebrated.

"Meritocratic" is an adjective that describes systems, processes, and environments where individual skill, effort, and achievement are the deciding factors in who succeeds, who is rewarded, and who rises. It stands opposed to systems where privilege, connections, birth, or favoritism carry the day.

At its most idealistic, it represents one of humanity's most cherished concepts of fairness: that what you earn matters more than what you inherit. At its most scrutinized, it reminds us that designing a genuinely fair system is far harder than simply declaring one, because the world people compete in is never truly level to begin with.

When you encounter the word in daily life, always ask two questions: What is the system rewarding? And did everyone have a fair chance to develop that merit in the first place? Those two questions will tell you whether something is genuinely meritocratic or merely claims to be.
10555:
Meritorious means deserving of praise, recognition, or reward because of genuine quality, effort, or excellence.

The heart of the word is "merit," which means worth or deserving. So when something is called meritorious, you're saying it has real, earned merit — not luck, not favoritism, not flattery. The praise is justified.

Think of it this way: if a student works incredibly hard, produces outstanding research, and submits a thesis that impresses even the toughest professors, that thesis could be called meritorious. It earned its recognition fairly.
What Makes It Different From Just "Good"

This is important. "Meritorious" is not just a fancy word for "good." It carries a stronger and more specific meaning.

"Good" is general. "Meritorious" means something has risen to a level where it genuinely deserves formal acknowledgment — a reward, an honor, or at the very least, deep respect. There is a sense that someone sat in judgment (officially or unofficially) and concluded: yes, this earns recognition.

It also implies the quality came from effort, skill, or moral conduct — not from being in the right place at the right time.

Meritorious is a formal word. You would rarely hear it in casual everyday conversation. You are far more likely to encounter it in:

  • Official documents and citations
  • Academic writing and reviews
  • Legal settings
  • Military or government contexts
  • Formal speeches or awards ceremonies

If your friend fixed your computer, you'd say "that was great of you," not "that was meritorious of you." But if a soldier was being honored for brave service, the official citation might read: "for meritorious conduct in the line of duty."
How It Is Used in Different Contexts

1. General Use
In everyday formal writing, it simply means praiseworthy and deserving of recognition.

  • "The committee acknowledged her meritorious contribution to public health."
  • "His meritorious efforts over the years finally led to a breakthrough."

The message is always: this person or thing genuinely earned its praise.

2. Military Use
This is one of the most common formal uses. Militaries around the world use the word to recognize soldiers whose service or conduct goes above and beyond what is normally expected.

  • "He was awarded the Meritorious Service Medal for his exceptional leadership."

Here, meritorious specifically signals that the conduct exceeded the standard — it wasn't just doing the job, it was doing it in a way that stood out and deserved official honor.

3. Legal Use
In law, "meritorious" takes on a precise and important meaning: a claim, case, or argument is meritorious if it has genuine legal substance — meaning there is a real, valid basis for it to be heard and considered by a court.

  • "The judge ruled that the defendant had a meritorious defense."
  • "Only meritorious claims will proceed to trial."

The opposite would be a "frivolous" claim — one with no real legal foundation, filed just to cause delays or harassment. A meritorious claim is the real thing; it has actual legal legs to stand on.

4. Academic Use
In academic or professional evaluations, meritorious work is work that stands out for its quality and deserves special recognition.

  • "The review panel considered only the most meritorious applications for the scholarship."

It's worth knowing that "meritorious" sits at a high level on the scale of praise. Here's a rough sense of scale, from weakest to strongest:

Adequate → Good → Commendable → Meritorious → Exemplary → Outstanding

It's not the absolute ceiling of praise, but it's firmly in the upper range. When you call something meritorious, you're not damning with faint praise — you're giving it serious, genuine credit.

• It does not mean boastful or self-congratulatory. Meritorious describes the quality of something, not someone showing off about it.
  • It does not simply mean "good" in a casual sense. The word always implies a level of formal worthiness.
  • It does not apply to things that succeeded by chance or by connections. If someone got a promotion because of their uncle, that's not meritorious — because the reward wasn't earned through genuine excellence.

Several words are close in meaning, but each has its own flavor:

  • Commendable — very similar, slightly less formal. You can use this in more everyday writing.
  • Praiseworthy — straightforward, plain-English equivalent. Less elevated in tone.
  • Laudable — similar formality to meritorious; often used for moral or humanitarian acts.
  • Admirable — focuses more on the emotional response of respect or admiration it inspires.
  • Exemplary — implies the thing is so good it sets an example others should follow. Slightly stronger.
The opposites of meritorious include: unworthy, dishonorable, blameworthy, disgraceful, reprehensible.
One-Line Summary to Lock It In

Meritorious = genuinely deserving of praise or reward because of real quality, effort, or excellence — not luck, not flattery.

If you remember that one idea, you have the word completely in your grasp.
10556:
Merriment means cheerful, lively fun — the kind filled with laughter, noise, and a light-hearted spirit. It describes the happy excitement that happens when people enjoy themselves freely and playfully, usually together.

If you picture a room full of people laughing, joking, playing games, and generally having a great time at a celebration — that whole atmosphere, that energy, is merriment.

The word isn't just about being happy. It carries a particular flavour. Three things define it:

1. It's active and expressive. Merriment isn't quiet or private. It shows itself — through laughter, noise, movement, and play. A person sitting alone feeling peaceful is content, not full of merriment.

2. It's light and playful, not deep or serious. Merriment is carefree. There's no weight to it. It's the feeling of a child running around at a birthday party, not the feeling of a mother holding her newborn for the first time (which is deep joy, not merriment).

3. It's almost always social. Merriment tends to arise among people — at gatherings, celebrations, parties, or any occasion where people come together and let themselves enjoy the moment. Lone merriment is rare and always worth noting.

Merriment is strongly associated with:

  • Festive occasions — Christmas, New Year's, weddings, harvest festivals, carnivals
  • Children at play — their laughter and games are often described this way
  • Celebrations and gatherings — any event where the mood lifts and people relax
  • Literature and storytelling — it's a favourite word in novels, poems, and older texts

You'll rarely hear someone use it in casual everyday speech ("I'm full of merriment today!"). It sounds natural in writing, descriptions, and slightly formal or literary contexts. But when you read it — in a novel, a news piece about a festival, or a poem — you'll recognise exactly what it means.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Understanding a word deeply means knowing how it sits among its neighbours:

Merriment vs. Happiness — Happiness is broad; it covers everything from quiet satisfaction to wild joy. Merriment is specific: it's the outward, playful, celebratory kind of happiness only.

Merriment vs. Joy — Joy can be private, still, and deep — a mother's joy, a spiritual feeling. Merriment is always expressed, lively, and social. Joy moves inward; merriment spills outward.

Merriment vs. Mirth — Mirth is very close to merriment, but mirth leans slightly more toward amusement and laughter specifically. If something is funny and everyone laughs, that's mirth. Merriment is wider — it covers the whole festive, playful atmosphere, not just the laughter.

Merriment vs. Hilarity — Hilarity is extreme amusement — uncontrollable, almost breathless laughter. Merriment is gentler and more sustained. A long, joyful party has merriment; the moment someone tells a brilliantly funny joke and the room explodes in laughter is hilarity.

Merriment vs. Revelry — Revelry is louder, wilder, and often implies excess — drinking, dancing, losing inhibitions. Merriment is warmer and more innocent. Children playing on Christmas morning are full of merriment; a loud street carnival going late into the night is revelry.

Merriment vs. Gaiety — These two are nearly interchangeable. Gaiety leans slightly more toward lightness of spirit and manner; merriment leans slightly more toward active fun and laughter. In most real-world use, the difference barely matters.

• Merriment is an uncountable noun. You cannot say "a merriment" or "three merriments." You use it without an article or with the/much/great/full of:
    • There was great merriment at the feast.
    • The hall was full of merriment.
    • Much merriment followed his joke.
  • The related adjective is merry ("a merry crowd"), and the related activity is merrymaking ("the merrymaking went on till midnight"). There is no single verb form; instead, English uses the phrase "to make merry" ("They made merry long into the night.")

• The children's merriment filled the house as they tore open their gifts.
  • There was much merriment at the wedding when the groom forgot his vows.
  • The sound of laughter and merriment drifted from the festival grounds.
  • She watched the merriment around her with a warm smile.
  • His unexpected joke caused great merriment among the guests.
  • The air was thick with merriment, music, and the smell of food.
Merriment = the lively, cheerful, outward fun — filled with laughter and playfulness — that people experience together at joyful, festive occasions.
10557:
Merry means cheerful, lively, and full of joy — especially the kind of joy that shows itself openly and is shared with others. A merry person is not just quietly happy inside; they are actively expressing that happiness — laughing, smiling, being playful, and spreading good cheer around them.

Think of it this way: if "happy" is a feeling, "merry" is happy in motion. It has energy to it.

This is the most important thing to understand about "merry." Many words mean happy, but they each have a different flavour. Here is how "merry" sits among them:

  • Happy is general and neutral. You can be happy alone, quietly, about anything.
  • Joyful is deeper and more emotional — sometimes even spiritual or overwhelming.
  • Cheerful is pleasant and upbeat, but calm.
  • Merry is light-hearted, festive, and lively. It belongs to celebrations, gatherings, and good times. It is the happiness of a party, a feast, a holiday — the kind where people are laughing, singing, clinking glasses, and having fun together.

Merry carries a sense of playful energy and festive warmth. It is bright, not heavy. It is social, not solitary. And it is almost always a positive, wholesome kind of feeling.

• "The children were merry and full of laughter on Christmas morning."
    → They were lively, cheerful, and visibly joyful.
  • "A merry group of friends gathered around the fireplace."
    → A cheerful, fun, warm group of people enjoying each other's company.
  • "She was in a merry mood all day."
    → She was light-hearted, upbeat, and full of good cheer.
  • "The hall was filled with merry music and dancing."
    → Lively, festive, joyful music that made people want to celebrate.

"Merry" is very strongly associated with celebrations and festivities. This is why the most famous use of this word is "Merry Christmas" — it means: may your Christmas be joyful, warm, lively, and full of good cheer. You could not say "Happy Christmas" and have it feel quite the same — "merry" brings that extra layer of festive energy and warmth that "happy" does not.

Similarly, the old phrase "eat, drink, and be merry" is a call to celebrate life, enjoy good food and company, and embrace cheerfulness. The word fits perfectly there because merriment is always tied to feasting, gathering, and shared pleasure.

In informal, mostly British English, "merry" can also be a gentle, polite way of saying someone is slightly drunk — not fully intoxicated, but loosened up and giggly from alcohol. This meaning works because alcohol at a party often makes people louder, more cheerful, and more playful — which is very "merry."

Example: "After two glasses of wine, she was feeling quite merry."
→ She was a little tipsy, in a light-hearted, happy way.

This secondary meaning is always mild and affectionate — it is never used to describe someone who is seriously drunk or behaving badly.

One very common expression is "to make merry," which means to celebrate, feast, and enjoy oneself with others. It is a slightly old-fashioned but still understood phrase.

  • "The whole village came together to make merry after the harvest."
    → Everyone gathered to celebrate and have a joyful, lively time.

Similarly, the noun form "merriment" means a state of lively, cheerful fun — the collective good cheer of a celebration. And "merrily" is the adverb: "They laughed merrily" means they laughed in a happy, carefree way.
Tone and Register: When Is This Word Used?

"Merry" is a slightly old-fashioned or literary word in everyday modern English. You would not typically say "I'm feeling merry today" in casual conversation — it would sound a little unusual. In day-to-day speech, people are more likely to say "happy," "cheerful," or "in a good mood."

However, "merry" is very much alive in set phrases (like "Merry Christmas"), in literature and poetry, in historical or period writing, and in a warm, storytelling tone. British English uses it more naturally than American English.

It also appears in traditional songs, folk tales, and old texts — phrases like "a merry old soul," "the merry month of May," or "Robin Hood and his merry men" (his cheerful, lively band of companions).
The Full Picture in One Sentence

Merry means: actively, visibly, and infectiously happy — in a light-hearted, festive, lively way — usually in a social or celebratory setting.

Whenever you see or hear this word, picture people laughing together at a party, or children dancing around a Christmas tree. That is the feeling "merry" carries.
10558: A mesa is a landform — a natural feature of the Earth's surface. Specifically, it is a hill or raised piece of land that has a flat, level top and steep, almost vertical sides (like cliffs). If you imagine a table sitting in the middle of an open desert, with a perfectly flat surface on top and sharp edges dropping straight down on all sides, you have a perfect mental picture of a mesa.

From a distance, a mesa looks like a large, isolated block of rock that has been sliced flat on top. The surrounding ground is much lower — you're essentially looking at a rocky "island" that rises steeply out of the landscape. The flat top can stretch for hundreds of meters or even several kilometers. The sides are not gentle slopes; they are sharp, dramatic drops made of exposed rock, often layered in shades of red, orange, brown, and tan.

The Earth's surface is made of layers of rock laid down over millions of years. Some layers are hard and resistant; others are soft and wear away more easily. Over a very long time, wind and water erode (wear away) the softer surrounding rock. But where there is a hard, resistant cap of rock on top, that section gets protected. The hard top shields what is directly below it from erosion, while everything around it slowly gets worn down. The result: a raised, flat-topped structure with steep sides — a mesa. This process is called differential erosion.

Mesas vary in size, but the flat top is always wider than the formation is tall. They are typically large enough that you could walk around on top for a while. The surrounding drop on all sides is usually significant — many meters to hundreds of meters.

Understanding a mesa is easier when you compare it to similar landforms:

Plateau — A plateau is also flat and elevated, but it is enormous in size — it can cover thousands of square kilometers and is often connected to nearby highlands. A mesa is much smaller and more isolated, standing alone like an island. Think of a plateau as a vast elevated plain, and a mesa as a much smaller chunk of land left behind after erosion.

Butte — A butte is essentially a smaller, narrower version of a mesa. The key difference is the ratio of width to height: on a mesa, the flat top is wider than the formation is tall; on a butte, the top is narrower than the formation is tall (making it look more like a tower or pillar). As erosion continues over time, a mesa can eventually shrink into a butte.

So the progression, from largest to smallest, goes: plateau → mesa → butte.

Mesas are most common in dry, arid regions — deserts and semi-deserts — because dry climates erode land slowly and in distinctive ways that leave these sharp, dramatic formations standing. The most famous mesas in the world are in the American Southwest, particularly in the states of Arizona, New Mexico, Colorado, and Utah. You'll also find them in parts of Africa, Australia, the Middle East, and South America.

A well-known example is Mesa Verde in Colorado, USA — the name literally means "green table" in Spanish, describing the flat, vegetation-covered top of the formation.

Because mesas rise steeply above the surrounding land, they are naturally defensible — it is very hard to approach one from the sides. Ancient peoples, particularly Native American communities like the Ancestral Puebloans, built their settlements on top of mesas for protection. The flat top provided space to live, farm, and survive, while the sheer cliffs acted as natural walls against enemies and predators.

The word "mesa" is used almost exclusively in its geographical sense — referring to this specific type of flat-topped landform. You might encounter it in:

  • Geography and earth science textbooks
  • Descriptions of landscapes in the American Southwest or other desert regions
  • Place names (Mesa, Arizona; Mesa Verde; Mesa Encantada, etc.)

It is not used metaphorically in common speech the way some landform words are. When someone says "mesa," they almost always mean the physical landform.

A mesa is an isolated, flat-topped, steep-sided raised landform, most commonly found in dry desert regions, formed when hard cap rock protects a section of land from erosion while the surrounding softer rock wears away — smaller than a plateau but larger and wider-topped than a butte.
10559:
To mesh means to fit together smoothly and work well as a unit — like pieces that interlock perfectly and function without friction.

The best image to hold in your mind is gear teeth. When two gears mesh, the teeth of one gear slide precisely into the gaps of the other. Neither gear fights the other. They lock in, turn together, and make something work. That interlocking, frictionless fit — that is the essence of "mesh."

In everyday language, "mesh" is used when abstract things — ideas, personalities, plans, styles, schedules, values — fit together in a compatible, harmonious way.

  • Their personalities mesh really well. → They get along naturally; their natures complement each other.
  • His work style doesn't mesh with the team's approach. → There's a mismatch; friction exists.
  • The two colour choices mesh beautifully. → The colours work together, not against each other.
  • Our schedules don't mesh this week. → The timings clash; they can't align.

Notice that things which "mesh" don't have to be identical — in fact, gear teeth only work because one has a tooth where the other has a gap. Mesh implies complementary fit, not sameness.

Physically, "mesh" describes what happens when parts of a mechanical system interlock:

  • The gears meshed smoothly after the engineer adjusted the alignment.

This is where the word's power comes from. In figurative use, you're borrowing that mechanical image of precise, interlocking, frictionless operation.

Intransitive (no object — things mesh on their own):

  • The two strategies just don't mesh.
  • Luckily, their visions meshed from day one.

Transitive (with an object — someone actively causes things to mesh):

  • She managed to mesh the two conflicting proposals into a single plan.
  • The director meshed the actors' different improvisation styles into one coherent scene.

In the transitive use, you are the one doing the work of making things fit together.

"Mesh" is equally powerful in the negative. When things fail to mesh, it means they grate against each other, conflict, or simply don't align:

  • Their worldviews never meshed, and the friendship eventually fell apart.
  • The new policy doesn't mesh with what the company claimed to stand for.

This negative use carries a clear sense of friction, incompatibility, or contradiction.

• Match → focuses on similarity or correspondence. Things that match look alike or pair neatly. A matching pair of socks. Mesh is about working together, not just looking alike.
  • Blend → focuses on things mixing until individual parts are less distinct, like colours blending into each other. Mesh preserves each part's identity — the gears stay separate gears — but they interlock functionally.
  • Align → means to come into the same line or position. Mesh is stronger: it implies not just alignment but active interlocking.

"Mesh" has a quiet, positive energy when used in the affirmative. It suggests things coming together naturally, without force — as if they were made for each other. When a writer says two characters "mesh effortlessly," you understand there's an organic chemistry at work, not something engineered or strained.

In the negative, it captures exactly why something isn't working — not that things are bad individually, but that they simply don't fit together.
